title: A Markov Chain Approach to Preference Alignment

paper.title: A Markov Chain Approach to Preference Alignment
paper.abstract:
Abstract We propose Markov Chain from Human Feedback (MCHF), an elementary approach for aligning generative models from pairwise human preferences. Unlike Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), which reduces comparisons to a scalar reward, and Nash Learning from Human Feedback (NLHF), which preserves pairwise utilities through a KL-regularized minimax optimization, MCHF uses pairwise preferences directly to define a transition mechanism over model outputs. Given a pairwise utility U ⁡ ( x , y ) U(x,y) , which quantifies human preference for y y over x x , and a reference probability distribution μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}} , we define a Markov kernel 𝖯 ⁡ ( x , d ​ y ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( U ⁡ ( x , y ) ) ​ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ ( d ​ y ) \mathsf{P}(x,dy)\propto\exp(U(x,y))\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}(dy) , and take the Markov chain starting from μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}} as an iterative alignment procedure. We show that MCHF converges geometrically fast to the stationary distribution, with a convergence rate governed by the seminorm ‖ U ‖ ⊕ = inf g , f ∈ L ∞ ​ ( μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) ‖ U − g ⊕ f ‖ ∞ \|U\|_{\oplus}=\inf_{g,f\in L^{\infty}(\mu_{\mathsf{ref}})}\|U-g\oplus f\|_{\infty} , which quantifies the non-transitive structure of the pairwise utility. We further show that a mirror-descent algorithm for NLHF satisfies an analogous structure-adaptive convergence guarantee. Finally, through a perturbation analysis, we prove that when ‖ U ‖ ⊕ \|U\|_{\oplus} is small, MCHF and NLHF agree up to first order around an RLHF solution, which yields a unified view of reward-based, game-theoretic, and Markovian approaches to alignment.
In particular, for two natural algorithms that converge to the MCHF/NLHF equilibria, we show that the first step of MCHF and NLHF recovers the RLHF solution based on the column-sum reward f ^ ​ ( y ) = ∫ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ ( 𝑑 x ) ​ U ​ ( x , y ) \hat{f}(y)=\int\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}(dx)U(x,y) , and starting from the second iteration, both algorithms incorporate the same linear functional of the residual U − ( − f ^ ) ⊕ f ^ U-(-\hat{f})\oplus\hat{f} , which captures the non-transitive structure of the pairwise utility U U .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Aligning AI systems with human preferences has become a central problem in modern machine learning, as large generative models are increasingly deployed in practical applications ( OpenAI, 2023 ; Gemini Team, Google, 2025 ; Anthropic, 2024 ) . In many alignment pipelines, human feedback is provided in the form of pairwise comparisons: given two candidate outputs, a human evaluator indicates which one is preferred. Such preference data are often easier to collect and prove more reliable than absolute numerical scores, as argued in several widely used alignment methods.

sections.heading: 1.1 Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)
sections.text: In Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), pairwise comparisons are typically used to fit a scalar reward model, often through a probabilistic preference model such as the Bradley–Terry or Luce (BTL) model ( Bradley and Terry, 1952 ; Luce, 1959 ) : 𝒫 ⁡ ( x ≺ y ) = σ sigmoid ​ ( R ⁡ ( y ) − R ⁡ ( x ) ) where σ sigmoid ​ ( t ) ≡ ( 1 + e − t ) − 1 . \displaystyle\mathcal{P}(x\prec y)=\sigma_{\text{sigmoid}}(R(y)-R(x))\quad\text{where}\quad\sigma_{\text{sigmoid}}(t)\equiv(1+e^{-t})^{-1}. (1) More precisely, given samples of pairwise comparisons { x i ≺ y i } i = 1 n \{x_{i}\prec y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} , assuming that they are drawn from the BTL model, one estimates the reward function R R by maximum likelihood estimation. The policy is then optimized against the learned reward R ^ \hat{R} , usually with a KL regularization term that keeps it close to a reference model μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}} ( Christiano et al., 2017 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Bai et al., 2022 ) : μ 𝖱𝖫 = argmax μ ( ∫ μ ⁡ ( 𝑑 x ) ​ R ^ ​ ( x ) − D 𝖪𝖫 ​ ( μ ∣ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) ) or μ 𝖱𝖫 ​ ( 𝑑 y ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( R ^ ​ ( y ) ) ​ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ ( 𝑑 y ) \displaystyle{\mu}_{\mathsf{RL}}=\argmax_{\mu}\Bigl(\int\mu(dx)\hat{R}(x)-D_{\mathsf{KL}}(\mu\mid\mu_{\mathsf{ref}})\Bigr)\quad\text{or}\quad\mu_{\mathsf{RL}}(dy)\propto\exp(\hat{R}(y))\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}(dy) In practice, this problem is often solved approximately using reinforcement-learning algorithms such as proximal policy optimization (PPO) ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) . More recently, several variants and alternatives to the standard RLHF pipeline have been proposed; see Rafailov et al. (2023) ; Ethayarajh et al. (2024) ; Meng et al. (2024) ; Gheshlaghi Azar et al. (2024) ; Huang et al. (2025) , among others. Although a variety of RLHF-style methods have been proposed, their ultimate goal remains to aggregate pairwise preference information to a single scalar reward and then tilt the reference distribution by the reward. At its core, the reward modeling relies on the strong assumption that human preference is determined by the single reward, as in the BTL model assumption ( 1 ), which imposes a strong structural restriction on the preference structure 𝒫 ⁡ ( x ≺ y ) \mathcal{P}(x\prec y) . In particular, such a model cannot capture genuinely cyclic preference patterns such as 𝒫 ⁡ ( x ≺ y ) > 1 / 2 , 𝒫 ⁡ ( y ≺ z ) > 1 / 2 , 𝒫 ⁡ ( z ≺ x ) > 1 / 2 \mathcal{P}(x\prec y)>1/2,\mathcal{P}(y\prec z)>1/2,\mathcal{P}(z\prec x)>1/2 . Furthermore, RLHF-style methods assume the existence of a single reward function representing aggregated human preference. In practice, preferences may vary across human annotators, and therefore cannot always be faithfully summarized by a homogeneous reward model. This limitation has motivated pluralistic alignment in the community, which tries to account for heterogeneous preferences explicitly ( Sorensen et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: 1.2 Nash Learning from Human Feedback (NLHF): a Game-Theoretic Approach
sections.text:
There have been a variety of attempts at incorporating preference information directly, without introducing an explicit single reward model. Among them, one influential example is the Nash Learning from Human Feedback (NLHF) ( Munos et al., 2024 ) . The key idea is to first learn the preference model ( x , y ) ↦ 𝒫 ⁡ ( x ≺ y ) (x,y)\mapsto\mathcal{P}(x\prec y) directly from a dataset of comparisons { x i ≺ y i } i = 1 n \{x_{i}\prec y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} , for instance by solving max ⁡ ∑ i = 1 n θ ⁡ log ⁡ 𝒫 θ ​ ( x i ≺ y i ) \max_{	heta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{P}_{	heta}(x_{i}\prec y_{i}) where { 𝒫 θ : 𝒳 × 𝒳 → [ 0 , 1 ] } \{\mathcal{P}_{	heta}:\mathcal{X}	imes\mathcal{X}	o[0,1]\} is a parametric class, typically represented by 𝒫 θ ​ ( x ≺ y ) = sigmoid ​ ( U θ ​ ( x , y ) ) \mathcal{P}_{	heta}(x\prec y)=	ext{sigmoid}(U_{	heta}(x,y)) (or more generally 𝒫 θ = Φ ∘ U θ \mathcal{P}_{	heta}=\Phi\circ U_{	heta} for an increasing link function Φ \Phi mapping to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] ), where U θ U_{	heta} is a neural network. Notice that when we further parametrize U θ U_{	heta} in additive form, U θ ​ ( x , y ) = − R θ ​ ( x ) + R θ ​ ( y ) U_{	heta}(x,y)=-R_{	heta}(x)+R_{	heta}(y) , then it is equivalent to the reward modelling by BTL model used in the RLHF pipeline. Given such a pairwise utility function U = U θ U=U_{	heta} , NLHF defines the aligned distribution through the following minimax optimization problem μ 𝖭𝖫 ∈ argmax μ min ν ​ ∬ ν ⁡ ( 𝑑 x ) ​ μ ​ ( 𝑑 y ) ​ U ​ ( x , y ) − D 𝖪𝖫 ​ ( μ ∣ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) + D 𝖪𝖫 ​ ( ν ∣ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) . \displaystyle{\mu}_{\mathsf{NL}}\in\argmax_{\mu}\min_{

More broadly, game-theoretic perspectives on alignment have led to formulations based on other solution concepts, such as Stackelberg games ( Pásztor et al., 2026 ; Chu et al., 2026 ) and multiplayer games ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . The NLHF paper ( Munos et al., 2024 ) argues that the Nash-equilibrium formulation is attractive because it can yield a more diverse distribution than reward-based alignment methods. A more refined analysis of this phenomenon has been developed through the lens of social choice theory (cf. Gölz et al. (2026) ; Shi et al. (2025) ). Nevertheless, because NLHF is formulated as a worst-case equilibrium against an adversarial opponent, it is intrinsically more pessimistic than reward-based alignment, and it is not always clear that such a pessimistic objective is the most appropriate one for fine-tuning generative models. Moreover, NLHF treats alignment as a simultaneous game, in which the two players, μ \mu and ν 
u , optimize a regularized zero-sum objective at the same time. In contrast, preference refinement can be more naturally viewed as a non-simultaneous, leader-follower procedure: given a current output, one samples a new output conditionally on it, favoring alternatives that are preferred to the current one. Figure 1: Workflow of alignment. We start from pairwise preference data, then we either construct a reward function (usually based on the BTL model) and run RLHF or construct a directed weighted graph and run MCHF (our proposal) or NLHF. Here, unlike the scalar reward, the weighted graph can preserve non-transitive/pairwise interaction structure in human preferences, and therefore MCHF/NLHF provide more flexible alignment methods than RLHF.

sections.heading: 1.3 Our contribution: a Markov Chain Approach
sections.text: Motivated by this viewpoint, we propose Markov Chain from Human Feedback (MCHF), a Markovian alignment approach that uses pairwise preference utilities directly through such a non-simultaneous formulation. Concretely, given a utility U ⁡ ( x , y ) U(x,y) , where larger values indicate that y y is preferred to x x , and a reference model μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}} , we define the Markov kernel 𝖯 \mathsf{P} by 𝖯 ⁡ ( x , d ​ y ) = exp ⁡ ( U ⁡ ( x , y ) ) Z ⁡ ( x ) ​ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ ( d ​ y ) , \mathsf{P}(x,dy)=\frac{\exp(U(x,y))}{Z(x)}\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}(dy), where Z ⁡ ( x ) Z(x) is the normalizing constant. Then, given a current distribution μ \mu , one step of MCHF updates it according to μ new ​ ( 𝑑 y ) = μ ​ 𝖯 ​ ( 𝑑 y ) = ∫ μ ⁡ ( 𝑑 x ) ​ 𝖯 ​ ( x , 𝑑 y ) . \mu_{\text{new}}(dy)=\mu\mathsf{P}(dy)=\int\mu(dx)\mathsf{P}(x,dy). Here, the kernel 𝖯 \mathsf{P} favors transitions from a current output x x to outputs y y that are preferred relative to x x , while the reference distribution μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}} preserves the structure, especially the support, of the reference distribution μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}} . Thus, in contrast to the simultaneous-game interpretation underlying NLHF, MCHF implements a non-simultaneous/leader-follower alignment procedure via the conditional sampling from the Markov kernel 𝖯 \mathsf{P} . This one-step update can also be iterated, starting from μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}} : μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ↦ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ 𝖯 ↦ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ 𝖯 2 ↦ ⋯ → μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ 𝖯 ∞ = μ 𝖬𝖢 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\mapsto\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\mathsf{P}\mapsto\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\mathsf{P}^{2}\mapsto\cdots\to\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\mathsf{P}^{\infty}=\mu_{\mathsf{MC}} Then, MCHF induces an interpolation path from the reference distribution to the stationary distribution μ 𝖬𝖢 \mu_{\mathsf{MC}} , which fully incorporates the pairwise preference utility U U . This iterative alignment procedure is inspired by classical spectral rank-aggregation methods ( Brin and Page, 1998 ; Negahban et al., 2017 ) , where one constructs a directed graph from pairwise comparisons and represents an aggregate ranking as the stationary distribution of a Markov chain on the graph (see Figure 1 ). Beyond introducing MCHF, our main theoretical contribution is to clarify its relationship with existing alignment methods such as NLHF and RLHF. A key observation is that, when the pairwise utility is written by an additive form U = g ⊕ f with ( g ⊕ f ) ​ ( x , y ) = g ⁡ ( x ) + f ⁡ ( y ) U=g\oplus f\quad\text{with}\quad(g\oplus f)(x,y)=g(x)+f(y) for some functions g g and f f , then the MCHF and NLHF equilibria based on such U U both reduce to the RLHF solution with reward f f : μ 𝖱𝖫 ​ ( f ) ​ ( d ​ y ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( f ⁡ ( y ) ) ​ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ ( d ​ y ) . \mu_{\mathsf{RL}}(f)(dy)\propto\exp(f(y))\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}(dy). This motivates us to compare MCHF and NLHF via a common perturbation framework: what are their first-order behaviors when U U is close to an additive pairwise utility g ⊕ f g\oplus f ? We address this question by introducing a seminorm ∥ ⋅ ∥ ⊕ \|\cdot\|_{\oplus} on L ∞ ​ ( μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ⊗ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) L^{\infty}(\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\otimes\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}) : ∀ U ∈ L ∞ ​ ( μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ⊗ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) , ‖ U ‖ ⊕ ≡ inf g , f ∈ L ∞ ​ ( μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) ‖ U − g ⊕ f ‖ ∞ , \displaystyle\forall U\in L^{\infty}(\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\otimes\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}),\quad\|U\|_{\oplus}\equiv\inf_{g,f\in L^{\infty}(\mu_{\mathsf{ref}})}\|U-g\oplus f\|_{\infty}, (3) which quantifies the non-additive or non-transitive structure of the pairwise preference utility U U . We then show that, when ‖ U ‖ ⊕ \|U\|_{\oplus} is small, RLHF provides a natural baseline corresponding to the transitive component of the pairwise utility, and around this baseline, NLHF and MCHF exhibit the same first-order structure, despite arising from different motivations: NLHF from a game-theoretic equilibrium and MCHF from a stationary distribution of a preference-driven Markov chain. This allows us to compare the three methods, RLHF, NLHF, and MCHF, within a common perturbative framework and to quantify how their differences depend on the non-transitive component of the preference utility U U . In this sense, we do not merely propose MCHF as an additional alignment algorithm, but also provide a unified view of reward-based, game-theoretic, and our Markovian approaches to preference alignment. Below, we summarize technical contributions of this paper.

sections.heading: Structure-Adaptive Convergence for MCHF and NLHF
sections.text: For MCHF, we prove the geometric convergence to the stationary distribution μ 𝖬𝖢 \mu_{\mathsf{MC}} : d 𝖳𝖵 ​ ( μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ 𝖯 t , μ 𝖬𝖢 ) ≤ d 𝖳𝖵 ​ ( μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 , μ 𝖬𝖢 ) ⋅ c ​ ( ‖ U ‖ ⊕ ) t with c ⁡ ( x ) ≡ min ⁡ ( 1 − e − 2 ​ x , x ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ) , \displaystyle d_{\mathsf{TV}}(\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\mathsf{P}^{t},\mu_{\mathsf{MC}})\leq d_{\mathsf{TV}}(\mu_{\mathsf{ref}},\mu_{\mathsf{MC}})\cdot c(\|U\|_{\oplus})^{t}\quad\text{with}\quad c(x)\equiv\min(1-e^{-2x},x)\in[0,1), where ‖ U ‖ ⊕ \|U\|_{\oplus} is the seminorm defined by ( 3 ). By the definition of the seminorm, we have ‖ U ‖ ⊕ ≤ ‖ U ‖ ∞ \|U\|_{\oplus}\leq\|U\|_{\infty} , but importantly, for natural choices of utilities and underlying human preference structures, it holds that ‖ U ‖ ⊕ ≪ ‖ U ‖ ∞ \|U\|_{\oplus}\ll\|U\|_{\infty} (see Example 2.2 - 2.3 ). Since the contraction rate c = c ⁡ ( ‖ U ‖ ⊕ ) c=c(\|U\|_{\oplus}) is an increasing function of ‖ U ‖ ⊕ \|U\|_{\oplus} , and the construction of our Markov kernel 𝖯 \mathsf{P} does not explicitly calculate the seminorm ‖ U ‖ ⊕ \|U\|_{\oplus} , this suggests that MCHF implicitly adapts to the additive/transitive structure of U U . To the best of our knowledge, our theoretical guarantee provides a sharper convergence guarantee than prior works (see Munos et al. (2024) ; Rosset et al. (2024) ; Tiapkin et al. (2025) and references therein), whose convergence rates usually depend on the naive norm ‖ U ‖ ∞ \|U\|_{\infty} .

This result gives a simple interpretation of the early-stage dynamics. sections.heading: 2 Definition of seminorm: measuring non-additive structure of utility
sections.text: Let U ⁡ ( x , y ) U(x,y) be a pairwise utility function that encodes preference information as follows: U ⁡ ( x , y ) is large ⟺ “a human is more likely to prefer y to x .” \displaystyle\text{$U(x,y)$ is large}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{``a human is more likely to prefer $y$ to $x$.''} Throughout this paper, we assume U ∈ L ∞ ​ ( μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ⊗ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) U\in L^{\infty}(\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\otimes\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}) , i.e., its L ∞ L^{\infty} norm with respect to the product measure is bounded. We now define a seminorm on L ∞ ​ ( μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ⊗ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) L^{\infty}(\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\otimes\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}) , which serves as a fundamental complexity measure for the alignment dynamics of MCHF and NLHF throughout this paper. Definition 2.1 . Define the seminorm ∥ ⋅ ∥ ⊕ \|\cdot\|_{\oplus} on L ∞ ​ ( μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ⊗ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) L^{\infty}(\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\otimes\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}) by ‖ U ‖ ⊕ = inf g , f ∈ L ∞ ​ ( μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) ‖ U − g ⊕ f ‖ ∞ , \|U\|_{\oplus}=\inf_{g,f\in L^{\infty}(\mu_{\mathsf{ref}})}\|U-g\oplus f\|_{\infty}, where ( g ⊕ f ) ​ ( x , y ) = g ⁡ ( x ) + f ⁡ ( y ) (g\oplus f)(x,y)=g(x)+f(y) . This seminorm ‖ U ‖ ⊕ \|U\|_{\oplus} captures the additive defect of the utility; the larger ‖ U ‖ ⊕ \|U\|_{\oplus} is, the more U U has a non-additive structure. We can also view this seminorm as the L ∞ L^{\infty} -distance to the class of additive functions { g ⊕ f : g , f ∈ L ∞ ( μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) } \{g\oplus f:g,f\in L^{\infty}(\mu_{\mathsf{ref}})\} . If the state space is finite, a similar yet more refined decomposition of pairwise comparison data, allowing for missing entries, has been studied in Jiang et al. (2011) . Note that ‖ U ‖ ⊕ ≤ ‖ U ‖ ∞ \|U\|_{\oplus}\leq\|U\|_{\infty} by the definition. In practice, the utility is often taken to be a possibly nonlinear transformation of the preference model 𝒫 ⁡ ( x ≺ y ) \mathcal{P}(x\prec y) , so the value of ‖ U ‖ ⊕ \|U\|_{\oplus} depends both on the nonlinear transformation and on the structure of 𝒫 ⁡ ( x ≺ y ) \mathcal{P}(x\prec y) . Importantly, the utility function need not be exactly additive, but there are natural situations in which it is approximately additive. Example 2.2 (Logit transform) . sections.heading: 4.1 Computational perspective
sections.text: There is a computational trade-off between the two approaches. MCHF requires sampling from the conditional distribution 𝖯 ⁡ ( x , ⋅ ) \mathsf{P}(x,\cdot) , whereas NLHF repeatedly solves KL-regularized optimization problems. As discussed in Section 3.2 , last-iterate convergence of NLHF typically requires adding a local regularization term η − 1 ​ D 𝖪𝖫 ​ ( μ ∣ μ t − 1 ) \eta^{-1}D_{\mathsf{KL}}(\mu\mid\mu_{t-1}) to the update, and because of this, each iteration requires both updating the reward function and sampling from a distribution involving a geometric mixture of μ t − 1 \mu_{t-1} and μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}} . This additional sampling step can be practically challenging. By contrast, MCHF requires implementing the conditional sampler 𝖯 ⁡ ( x , d ​ y ) \mathsf{P}(x,dy) , but this sampler needs to be implemented only once. Once such a sampling block is available, the alignment procedure simply consists of repeatedly applying the same Markov kernel. In this sense, MCHF can be viewed as attaching a preference-guided conditional sampling module on top of the existing architecture that generates samples from μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}} ; see Figure 2 .

sections.heading: 4.2 Coupling perspective and inference time refinement
sections.text: Another key difference between NLHF and MCHF lies in their algorithms. For the sake of simplicity, we focus on the antisymmetric utility U U . Suppose μ 0 \mu^{0} is a current distribution, and we update it via the following two different rules: μ 𝖬𝖢 1 = μ 0 𝖯 , μ 𝖭𝖫 1 ∈ argmax μ ∫ μ 0 ( d x ) μ ( d y ) U ( x , y ) − D 𝖪𝖫 ( μ ∣ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) \displaystyle\mu_{\mathsf{MC}}^{1}=\mu^{0}\mathsf{P},\qquad\mu_{\mathsf{NL}}^{1}\in\argmax_{\mu}\int\mu^{0}(dx)\mu(dy)U(x,y)-D_{\mathsf{KL}}(\mu\mid\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}) Note that μ 𝖬𝖢 \mu_{\mathsf{MC}} is the stationary point of the first update, while μ 𝖭𝖫 \mu_{\mathsf{NL}} is the equilibrium of the second update since we are assuming that U U is antisymmetric now. To compare these two updates, consider the couplings induced by MCHF and NLHF: π 𝖬𝖢 ​ ( d ​ x , d ​ y ) = μ 0 ​ ( d ​ x ) ​ 𝖯 ​ ( x , d ​ y ) , π 𝖭𝖫 ​ ( d ​ x , d ​ y ) = μ 0 ​ ( d ​ x ) ​ μ 𝖭𝖫 1 ​ ( d ​ y ) . \pi_{\mathsf{MC}}(dx,dy)=\mu^{0}(dx)\mathsf{P}(x,dy),\quad\pi_{\mathsf{NL}}(dx,dy)=\mu^{0}(dx)\mu_{\mathsf{NL}}^{1}(dy). The second marginal of these couplings is precisely μ 𝖬𝖢 1 \mu_{\mathsf{MC}}^{1} and μ 𝖭𝖫 1 \mu_{\mathsf{NL}}^{1} , respectively. Then, by the definition of Markov kernel 𝖯 \mathsf{P} and the update rule of μ 𝖭𝖫 1 \mu_{\mathsf{NL}}^{1} , π 𝖬𝖢 \pi_{\mathsf{MC}} and π 𝖭𝖫 \pi_{\mathsf{NL}} maximize the same objective function: F ( π ) = ∬ U ( x , y ) π ( d x , d y ) − D 𝖪𝖫 ( π | | μ 0 ⊗ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) , F(\pi)=\iint U(x,y)\pi(dx,dy)-D_{\mathsf{KL}}(\pi||\mu^{0}\otimes\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}), but over different feasible spaces of couplings: π 𝖬𝖢 = argmax ∫ π ⁡ ( ⋅ , 𝑑 y ) = μ 0 ​ ( ⋅ ) F ​ ( π ) , π 𝖭𝖫 = argmax ∃ μ , π = μ 0 ⊗ μ F ​ ( π ) . \displaystyle\pi_{\mathsf{MC}}=\argmax_{\int\pi(\cdot,dy)=\mu^{0}(\cdot)}F(\pi),\quad\pi_{\mathsf{NL}}=\argmax_{\exists\mu,\pi=\mu^{0}\otimes\mu}F(\pi). Thus, the MCHF coupling optimizes over a larger class of couplings than that of NLHF, and in this sense the coupling induced by MCHF can extract more utility from the preference structure than the product coupling induced by NLHF. This coupling perspective also highlights a practical difference between the two methods. Since MCHF produces a conditional distribution 𝖯 ⁡ ( x , ⋅ ) \mathsf{P}(x,\cdot) given the current output x x , it naturally supports an inference-time refinement procedure: one may repeatedly refine a model output by sampling from 𝖯 ⁡ ( x , ⋅ ) \mathsf{P}(x,\cdot) until the user is satisfied. This is reminiscent of the inference-time refinement mechanism discussed in Stackelberg game-based alignment ( Pásztor et al., 2026 ) . By contrast, the NLHF update directly produces a marginal distribution and therefore does not provide the same conditional refinement mechanism. Below we provide a simple example to highlight the benefit of MCHF (note that this example is used in Pásztor et al. (2026) to highlight the benefit of conditional alignment). In Appendix F , we extend the above rock-paper-scissors game to a general reference measure μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}} and general antisymmetric utility U U , and show that we can reduce the number of samples needed to get a desired output by running our Markov kernel 𝖯 γ ​ ( x , d ​ y ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( γ ​ U ​ ( x , y ) ) ​ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ ( d ​ y ) \mathsf{P}_{\gamma}(x,dy)\propto\exp(\gamma U(x,y))\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}(dy) for a finite γ \gamma . sections.heading: 4.4 Stability under perturbation of utilities
sections.text: Finally, en route to the proof of Theorem 4.2 , we obtain a stability result for MCHF and NLHF equilibria under the perturbation of utilities. This stability property is important in practice, since the utility function U U may be updated as new preference data become available. We may also consider a setting in which U U is taken to be an increasing transformation of the preference model 𝒫 ⁡ ( x ≺ y ) \mathcal{P}(x\prec y) , which is itself estimated, for example, by logistic regression as in the original paper Munos et al. (2024) . In this case, estimation error in 𝒫 \mathcal{P} induces a perturbation in U U . It is therefore important to understand how such perturbations affect the resulting equilibrium. Theorem 4.6 (Stability under perturbation of utilities) . Then, there exists a constant C R C_{R} , depending only on R R , such that for each ∗ ∈ { 𝖬𝖢 , 𝖭𝖫 } *\in\{\mathsf{MC},\mathsf{NL}\} , we have sup U , U ^ ∈ B ⊕ ∞ ​ ( R ) d 𝖳𝖵 ​ ( μ ∗ ​ ( U ) , μ ∗ ​ ( U ^ ) ) ‖ U − U ^ ‖ ∞ ≤ C R . \sup_{U,\hat{U}\in B^{\infty}_{\oplus}(R)}\frac{d_{\mathsf{TV}}(\mu_{*}(U),\mu_{*}(\hat{U}))}{\|U-\hat{U}\|_{\infty}}\leq C_{R}. Since ‖ U ‖ ⊕ ≤ ‖ U ‖ ∞ \|U\|_{\oplus}\leq\|U\|_{\infty} , this ball includes the usual L ∞ L^{\infty} -ball of radius R R . Furthermore, B ⊕ ∞ ​ ( R ) B^{\infty}_{\oplus}(R) is invariant under the addition of additive structure: if U ∈ B ⊕ ∞ ​ ( R ) U\in B^{\infty}_{\oplus}(R) , then U + g ⊕ f ∈ B ⊕ ∞ ​ ( R ) U+g\oplus f\in B^{\infty}_{\oplus}(R) for any g , f ∈ L ∞ g,f\in L^{\infty} . sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: In this paper, we proposed MCHF, an alternative framework for aligning generative models with human preferences by constructing a Markov kernel directly from pairwise preference information. We showed that the resulting Markov chain converges geometrically fast to its stationary distribution, with a contraction rate governed by the seminorm ‖ U ‖ ⊕ \|U\|_{\oplus} , which captures the non-transitive component of the pairwise utility. We further showed that the mirror-descent algorithm for NLHF, under an appropriate choice of step size, satisfies an analogous structure-adaptive convergence guarantee. Finally, through a perturbation analysis, we proved that when ‖ U ‖ ⊕ \|U\|_{\oplus} is small, MCHF and NLHF agree up to first order around the RLHF solution. These results provide a unified perspective on reward-based, game-theoretic, and Markovian approaches to preference alignment. It would also be interesting to investigate how the pairwise utility should be designed so that the aligned distribution induced by MCHF satisfies desirable axioms from social choice theory. Related questions have been studied for RLHF and NLHF; see, for example, Liu et al. (2025) ; Gölz et al. (2026) and the references therein. We leave a systematic social-choice-theoretic analysis of MCHF to future work. Our analysis in this paper was primarily theoretical, and we leave the practical implementation of MCHF for future work. To run the Markov chain in practice, one needs to sample from the conditional distribution 𝖯 ⁡ ( x , d ​ y ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( U ⁡ ( x , y ) ) ​ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ ( d ​ y ) \mathsf{P}(x,dy)\propto\exp(U(x,y))\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}(dy) given the current output x x . This problem can be viewed as a conditional analogue of sampling from an RLHF solution of the form μ 𝖱𝖫 ​ ( d ​ y ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( r ⁡ ( y ) ) ​ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ ( d ​ y ) . \mu_{\mathsf{RL}}(dy)\propto\exp(r(y))\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}(dy). Recent developments for sampling from such reward-tilted or unnormalized distributions, including rejection-sampling-based approaches Liu et al. (2025) , SDE-based methods such as diffusion models (see Uehara et al. (2024) and the references therein), and a recent Monge–Ampère PDE sampler Deb and Liang (2025) , provide promising tools for this purpose. Developing scalable implementations of MCHF by adapting these techniques to the Markov kernel 𝖯 ⁡ ( x , d ​ y ) \mathsf{P}(x,dy) is an important direction for future work.

sections.heading: Appendix D Fréchet Differentiability and Stability
sections.text: This section provides the technical ingredients needed for the analysis of the alignment dynamics in Section 4.3 , in particular Proposition 4.3 and Theorem 4.5 . Our main goal is to establish the uniform Fréchet differentiability result stated in Theorem 4.2 , together with an explicit derivative formula. To this end, we organize this section as follows: • Section D.1 : Fréchet differentiability and derivative formulas for MCHF and NLHF; see Theorems D.1 and D.3 , respectively. • Section D.2 : The stability estimate introduced in Theorem 4.6 . • Section D.3 : Uniform Fréchet differentiability; namely, the proof of Theorem 4.2 for MCHF and NLHF. Readers primarily interested in the consequences for the alignment dynamics may read the statements of Theorems D.1 and D.3 , skip the other theorems and technical proofs, and proceed directly to Appendix E .

sections.text: Next, we claim the stability of the NLHF solution μ 𝖭𝖫 \mu_{\mathsf{NL}} . Theorem D.6 (Stability of NLHF equilibrium) . There exists an absolute constant C C such that, for any U , U ^ ∈ L ∞ ​ ( μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ⊗ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) U,\hat{U}\in L^{\infty}(\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\otimes\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}) , d 𝖳𝖵 ​ ( μ 𝖭𝖫 ​ ( U ) , μ 𝖭𝖫 ​ ( U ^ ) ) ≤ C ⁡ ( 1 + ‖ U ‖ ⊕ 6 + ‖ U ^ ‖ ⊕ 6 ) ​ ‖ U − U ^ ‖ ∞ . d_{\mathsf{TV}}\bigl(\mu_{\mathsf{NL}}(U),\mu_{\mathsf{NL}}(\hat{U})\bigr)\leq C\bigl(1+\|U\|_{\oplus}^{6}+\|\hat{U}\|_{\oplus}^{6}\bigr)\|U-\hat{U}\|_{\infty}. sections.heading: D.3 Uniform Fréchet differentiability
sections.text: We have seen in Section D.1 that MCHF and NLHF are both Fréchet differentiable; there exists derivatives D ​ p ∗ ​ ( U ) Dp_{*}(U) for ∗ ∈ { 𝖬𝖢 , 𝖭𝖫 } *\in\{\mathsf{MC},\mathsf{NL}\} such that ∀ U ∈ L ∞ ​ ( μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ⊗ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) , lim ‖ E ‖ ∞ → 0 ‖ p ∗ ​ ( U + E ) − p ∗ ​ ( U ) − D ​ p ∗ ​ ( U ) ​ [ E ] ‖ 1 ‖ E ‖ ∞ = 0 . \displaystyle\forall U\in L^{\infty}(\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\otimes\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}),\quad\lim_{\|E\|_{\infty}\to 0}\frac{\|p_{*}(U+E)-p_{*}(U)-Dp_{*}(U)[E]\|_{1}}{\|E\|_{\infty}}=0. Now we aim to make this convergence result uniform for all U U such that ‖ U ‖ ⊕ ≤ R \|U\|_{\oplus}\leq R for a fixed constant R R , i.e., we aim to show the above convergence with sup ‖ U ‖ ⊕ ≤ R \sup_{\|U\|_{\oplus}\leq R} inside lim ‖ E ‖ ∞ → 0 \lim_{\|E\|_{\infty}\to 0} . Lemma D.10 . ‖ J p − J q ‖ ∞ → 1 = sup ‖ f ‖ ∞ ≤ 1 ‖ ( J p − J q ) ​ f ‖ 1 ≤ 3 ​ ‖ p − q ‖ 1 \|J_{p}-J_{q}\|_{\infty\to 1}=\sup_{\|f\|_{\infty}\leq 1}\|(J_{p}-J_{q})f\|_{1}\leq 3\|p-q\|_{1} for any p , q ∈ Δ ∞ p,q\in\Delta^{\infty} Proof. For any f ∈ L ∞ f\in L^{\infty} , writing J p ​ f = p ⊙ f − p ⋅ ⟨ p , f ⟩ J_{p}f=p\odot f-p\cdot\langle p,f\rangle , ( J p − J q ) ​ f \displaystyle(J_{p}-J_{q})f = ( p − q ) ⊙ f − ( p − q ) ⋅ ⟨ p , f ⟩ − q ⋅ ⟨ p − q , f ⟩ \displaystyle=(p-q)\odot f-(p-q)\cdot\langle p,f\rangle-q\cdot\langle p-q,f\rangle Using Hölder’s inequality with ‖ p ‖ 1 = ‖ q ‖ 1 = 1 \|p\|_{1}=\|q\|_{1}=1 , one can show that the L 1 L^{1} norm of each term on RHS is bounded by ‖ p − q ‖ 1 ​ ‖ f ‖ ∞ \|p-q\|_{1}\|f\|_{\infty} . Thus, by the triangle inequality, complete the proof. ∎

sections.text: Lemma D.11 . Let A U A_{U} and h U h_{U} as A U = I − P U ⋆ , h U , E ​ ( y ) = ∫ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ ( 𝑑 x ) ​ p 𝖬𝖢 ​ ( U ) ​ ( x ) ​ [ J P U ​ ( x , ⋅ ) ​ E ​ ( x , ⋅ ) ] ​ ( y ) A_{U}=I-P_{U}^{\star},\quad h_{U,E}(y)=\int\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}(dx)p_{\mathsf{MC}}(U)(x)[J_{P_{U}(x,\cdot)}E(x,\cdot)](y) so that D ​ p 𝖬𝖢 ​ ( U ) ​ [ E ] = ( A U ∣ L 0 1 ) − 1 ​ h U , E Dp_{\mathsf{MC}}(U)[E]=\bigl(A_{U}\mid_{L_{0}^{1}}\bigr)^{-1}h_{U,E} . Then, using Lemma B.3 , we have esssup x ‖ P V ​ ( x , ⋅ ) − P U ​ ( x , ⋅ ) ‖ 1 ≤ esssup x ‖ V ⁡ ( x , ⋅ ) − U ⁡ ( x , ⋅ ) ‖ ∞ = ‖ U − V ‖ ∞ \esssup_{x}\|P_{V}(x,\cdot)-P_{U}(x,\cdot)\|_{1}\leq\esssup_{x}\|V(x,\cdot)-U(x,\cdot)\|_{\infty}=\|U-V\|_{\infty} and hence ‖ A U − A V ‖ 1 → 1 = ‖ P V ⋆ − P U ⋆ ‖ 1 → 1 ≤ ‖ U − V ‖ ∞ \|A_{U}-A_{V}\|_{1\to 1}=\|P_{V}^{\star}-P_{U}^{\star}\|_{1\to 1}\leq\|U-V\|_{\infty} . Therefore, we obtain ‖ ( ( A U | L 0 1 ) − 1 − ( A V | L 0 1 ) − 1 ) ∣ L 0 1 ‖ 1 → 1 ≤ exp ⁡ ( 2 ​ ‖ U ‖ ⊕ ) ​ exp ⁡ ( 2 ​ ‖ V ‖ ⊕ ) ​ ‖ U − V ‖ ∞ \displaystyle\Bigl\|\bigl((A_{U}|_{L_{0}^{1}})^{-1}-(A_{V}|_{L_{0}^{1}})^{-1}\bigr)\mid_{L_{0}^{1}}\Bigr\|_{1\to 1}\leq\exp(2\|U\|_{\oplus})\exp(2\|V\|_{\oplus})\|U-V\|_{\infty} Next, we bound h V , E h_{V,E} . Using ‖ J p ‖ ∞ → 1 ≤ 1 \|J_{p}\|_{\infty\to 1}\leq 1 from Lemma D.7 , whenever ‖ E ‖ ∞ ≤ 1 \|E\|_{\infty}\leq 1 , ‖ h V , E ‖ 1 ≤ ∫ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ ( 𝑑 x ) ​ p 𝖬𝖢 ​ ( V ) ​ ( x ) ​ ‖ J P V ​ ( x , ⋅ ) ​ E ​ ( x , ⋅ ) ‖ 1 ≤ esssup x ‖ J P V ​ ( x , ⋅ ) ​ E ​ ( x , ⋅ ) ‖ 1 ≤ 1 . \displaystyle\|h_{V,E}\|_{1}\leq\int\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}(dx)p_{\mathsf{MC}}(V)(x)\|J_{P_{V}(x,\cdot)}E(x,\cdot)\|_{1}\leq\esssup_{x}\|J_{P_{V}(x,\cdot)}E(x,\cdot)\|_{1}\leq 1. Hence, ‖ ( ( A U | L 0 1 ) − 1 − ( A V | L 0 1 ) − 1 ) ​ h V , E ‖ 1 ≤ exp ⁡ ( 2 ​ ‖ U ‖ ⊕ + 2 ​ ‖ V ‖ ⊕ ) ​ ‖ U − V ‖ ∞ . \displaystyle\bigl\|\bigl((A_{U}|_{L_{0}^{1}})^{-1}-(A_{V}|_{L_{0}^{1}})^{-1}\bigr)h_{V,E}\bigr\|_{1}\leq\exp(2\|U\|_{\oplus}+2\|V\|_{\oplus})\|U-V\|_{\infty}. It remains to bound h U , E − h V , E h_{U,E}-h_{V,E} . We write h U , E − h V , E \displaystyle h_{U,E}-h_{V,E} = ∫ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ ( 𝑑 x ) ​ { p 𝖬𝖢 ​ ( U ) ​ ( x ) − p 𝖬𝖢 ​ ( V ) ​ ( x ) } ​ J P U ​ ( x , ⋅ ) ​ E ​ ( x , ⋅ ) \displaystyle=\int\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}(dx)\{p_{\mathsf{MC}}(U)(x)-p_{\mathsf{MC}}(V)(x)\}J_{P_{U}(x,\cdot)}E(x,\cdot) + ∫ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ( d x ) p 𝖬𝖢 ( V ) ( x ) { J P U ​ ( x , ⋅ ) − J P V ​ ( x , ⋅ ) } E ( x , ⋅ ) . \displaystyle+\int\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}(dx)p_{\mathsf{MC}}(V)(x)\{J_{P_{U}(x,\cdot)}-J_{P_{V}(x,\cdot)}\}E(x,\cdot). For the first term, using again esssup x ‖ J P U ​ ( x , ⋅ ) ​ E ​ ( x , ⋅ ) ‖ 1 ≤ ‖ E ‖ ∞ ≤ 1 \esssup_{x}\|J_{P_{U}(x,\cdot)}E(x,\cdot)\|_{1}\leq\|E\|_{\infty}\leq 1 , we get ‖ ∫ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ ( 𝑑 x ) ​ { p 𝖬𝖢 ​ ( U ) ​ ( x ) − p 𝖬𝖢 ​ ( V ) ​ ( x ) } ​ J P U ​ ( x , ⋅ ) ​ E ​ ( x , ⋅ ) ‖ 1 ≤ ‖ p 𝖬𝖢 ​ ( U ) − p 𝖬𝖢 ​ ( V ) ‖ 1 . \displaystyle\Bigl\|\int\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}(dx)\{p_{\mathsf{MC}}(U)(x)-p_{\mathsf{MC}}(V)(x)\}J_{P_{U}(x,\cdot)}E(x,\cdot)\Bigr\|_{1}\leq\|p_{\mathsf{MC}}(U)-p_{\mathsf{MC}}(V)\|_{1}. By Corollary D.5 , ‖ p 𝖬𝖢 ​ ( U ) − p 𝖬𝖢 ​ ( V ) ‖ 1 ≤ exp ⁡ { 2 ​ ( ‖ U ‖ ⊕ ∧ ‖ V ‖ ⊕ ) } ​ ‖ U − V ‖ ∞ . \displaystyle\|p_{\mathsf{MC}}(U)-p_{\mathsf{MC}}(V)\|_{1}\leq\exp\{2(\|U\|_{\oplus}\wedge\|V\|_{\oplus})\}\|U-V\|_{\infty}. Thus, the first term is bounded by exp ⁡ { 2 ​ ( ‖ U ‖ ⊕ ∧ ‖ V ‖ ⊕ ) } ​ ‖ U − V ‖ ∞ \exp\{2(\|U\|_{\oplus}\wedge\|V\|_{\oplus})\}\|U-V\|_{\infty} . For the second term, using ‖ J p − J q ‖ ∞ → 1 ≤ 3 ​ ‖ p − q ‖ 1 \|J_{p}-J_{q}\|_{\infty\to 1}\leq 3\|p-q\|_{1} in Lemma D.10 , ‖ ∫ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ ( 𝑑 x ) ​ p 𝖬𝖢 ​ ( V ) ​ ( x ) ​ { J P U ​ ( x , ⋅ ) − J P V ​ ( x , ⋅ ) } ​ E ​ ( x , ⋅ ) ‖ 1 \displaystyle\Bigl\|\int\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}(dx)p_{\mathsf{MC}}(V)(x)\{J_{P_{U}(x,\cdot)}-J_{P_{V}(x,\cdot)}\}E(x,\cdot)\Bigr\|_{1} ≤ 3 ​ esssup x ‖ P U ​ ( x , ⋅ ) − P V ​ ( x , ⋅ ) ‖ 1 \displaystyle\leq 3\esssup_{x}\|P_{U}(x,\cdot)-P_{V}(x,\cdot)\|_{1} Using again esssup x ‖ P U ​ ( x , ⋅ ) − P V ​ ( x , ⋅ ) ‖ 1 ≤ ‖ U − V ‖ ∞ \esssup_{x}\|P_{U}(x,\cdot)-P_{V}(x,\cdot)\|_{1}\leq\|U-V\|_{\infty} , the second term is bounded by 3 ​ ‖ U − V ‖ ∞ 3\|U-V\|_{\infty} . For any constant R ≥ 0 R\geq 0 , lim ‖ E ‖ ∞ → 0 sup ‖ U ‖ ⊕ ≤ R ‖ p 𝖬𝖢 ​ ( U + E ) − p 𝖬𝖢 ​ ( U ) − D ​ p 𝖬𝖢 ​ ( U ) ​ [ E ] ‖ 1 ‖ E ‖ ∞ = 0 . \displaystyle\lim_{\|E\|_{\infty}\to 0}\sup_{\|U\|_{\oplus}\leq R}\frac{\|p_{\mathsf{MC}}(U+E)-p_{\mathsf{MC}}(U)-Dp_{\mathsf{MC}}(U)[E]\|_{1}}{\|E\|_{\infty}}=0. Proof. Fix U ∈ L ∞ ​ ( μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ⊗ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) U\in L^{\infty}(\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\otimes\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}) . sections.text: Lemma D.13 . There exists a universal constant c > 0 c>0 such that for any U , V ∈ L ∞ ​ ( μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ⊗ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) U,V\in L^{\infty}(\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\otimes\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}) , sup ‖ E ‖ ∞ ≤ 1 ‖ D ​ p 𝖭𝖫 ​ ( U ) ​ [ E ] − D ​ p 𝖭𝖫 ​ ( V ) ​ [ E ] ‖ 1 ≤ c ⁡ ( 1 + ‖ U ‖ ⊕ c + ‖ V ‖ ⊕ c ) ​ ‖ U − V ‖ ∞ . \displaystyle\sup_{\|E\|_{\infty}\leq 1}\|Dp_{\mathsf{NL}}(U)[E]-Dp_{\mathsf{NL}}(V)[E]\|_{1}\leq c(1+\|U\|_{\oplus}^{c}+\|V\|_{\oplus}^{c})\|U-V\|_{\infty}. Proof. The proof follows the same structure as that of Lemma D.11 . Write p U = p 𝖭𝖫 ​ ( U ) p_{U}=p_{\mathsf{NL}}(U) , q U = q 𝖭𝖫 ​ ( U ) q_{U}=q_{\mathsf{NL}}(U) and define A U = I + J p U ​ U ⋆ ​ J q U ​ U , h U , E = J p U ​ E ⋆ ​ q U − J p U ​ U ⋆ ​ J q U ​ E ​ p U . A_{U}=I+J_{p_{U}}U^{\star}J_{q_{U}}U,\qquad h_{U,E}=J_{p_{U}}E^{\star}q_{U}-J_{p_{U}}U^{\star}J_{q_{U}}Ep_{U}. By Theorem D.3 , D ​ p 𝖭𝖫 ​ ( U ) ​ [ E ] = A U − 1 ​ h U , E , Dp_{\mathsf{NL}}(U)[E]=A_{U}^{-1}h_{U,E}, so we decompose D ​ p 𝖭𝖫 ​ ( U ) ​ [ E ] − D ​ p 𝖭𝖫 ​ ( V ) ​ [ E ] \displaystyle Dp_{\mathsf{NL}}(U)[E]-Dp_{\mathsf{NL}}(V)[E] = A U − 1 ​ ( A V − A U ) ​ A V − 1 ​ h V , E + A U − 1 ​ ( h U , E − h V , E ) , \displaystyle=A_{U}^{-1}(A_{V}-A_{U})A_{V}^{-1}h_{V,E}+A_{U}^{-1}(h_{U,E}-h_{V,E}), where we used the identity A U − 1 − A V − 1 = A U − 1 ​ ( A V − A U ) ​ A V − 1 . A_{U}^{-1}-A_{V}^{-1}=A_{U}^{-1}(A_{V}-A_{U})A_{V}^{-1}. We now collect the bounds needed for the two terms. First, by Lemma D.7 and Lemma D.10 , for any K ∈ L ∞ ​ ( μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ⊗ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) K\in L^{\infty}(\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\otimes\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}) and any p , q ∈ Δ ∞ p,q\in\Delta^{\infty} , we have ∀ h ∈ L 1 , ‖ J p ​ K ​ h ‖ 1 \displaystyle\forall h\in L^{1},\quad\|J_{p}Kh\|_{1} ≤ ‖ K ​ h ‖ ∞ ≤ ‖ K ‖ ∞ ​ ‖ h ‖ 1 \displaystyle\leq\|Kh\|_{\infty}\leq\|K\|_{\infty}\|h\|_{1} ∀ h ∈ L 1 , ‖ ( J p − J q ) ​ K ​ h ‖ 1 \displaystyle\forall h\in L^{1},\quad\|(J_{p}-J_{q})Kh\|_{1} ≤ 3 ​ ‖ p − q ‖ 1 ​ ‖ K ​ h ‖ ∞ ≤ 3 ​ ‖ p − q ‖ 1 ​ ‖ K ‖ ∞ ​ ‖ h ‖ 1 . \displaystyle\leq 3\|p-q\|_{1}\|Kh\|_{\infty}\leq 3\|p-q\|_{1}\|K\|_{\infty}\|h\|_{1}. Third, by the L 1 L^{1} -bound of the inverse operator from Lemma D.8 , with additive parts removed as in the proof of Theorem D.6 , ∀ h ∈ L 0 1 , ‖ A U − 1 ​ h ‖ 1 ≤ c ⁡ ( 1 + ‖ U ‖ ⊕ 5 ) ​ ‖ h ‖ 1 , ‖ A V − 1 ​ h ‖ 1 ≤ c ⁡ ( 1 + ‖ V ‖ ⊕ 5 ) ​ ‖ h ‖ 1 . \forall h\in L_{0}^{1},\quad\|A_{U}^{-1}h\|_{1}\leq c(1+\|U\|_{\oplus}^{5})\|h\|_{1},\qquad\|A_{V}^{-1}h\|_{1}\leq c(1+\|V\|_{\oplus}^{5})\|h\|_{1}. Similarly, ‖ h V , E ‖ 1 ≤ ‖ J p V ​ E ⋆ ​ q V ‖ 1 + ‖ J p V ​ V ⋆ ​ J q V ​ E ​ p V ‖ 1 ≤ ( 1 + ‖ V ‖ ⊕ ) ​ ‖ E ‖ ∞ , \|h_{V,E}\|_{1}\leq\|J_{p_{V}}E^{\star}q_{V}\|_{1}+\|J_{p_{V}}V^{\star}J_{q_{V}}Ep_{V}\|_{1}\leq(1+\|V\|_{\oplus})\|E\|_{\infty}, and ‖ h U , E − h V , E ‖ 1 ≤ c ⁡ ( 1 + ‖ U ‖ ⊕ c + ‖ V ‖ ⊕ c ) ​ ‖ U − V ‖ ∞ ​ ‖ E ‖ ∞ . \|h_{U,E}-h_{V,E}\|_{1}\leq c\bigl(1+\|U\|_{\oplus}^{c}+\|V\|_{\oplus}^{c}\bigr)\|U-V\|_{\infty}\|E\|_{\infty}. The second bound follows by expanding h U , E − h V , E \displaystyle h_{U,E}-h_{V,E} = { J p U ​ E ⋆ ​ q U − J p V ​ E ⋆ ​ q V } − { J p U ​ U ⋆ ​ J q U ​ E ​ p U − J p V ​ V ⋆ ​ J q V ​ E ​ p V } , \displaystyle=\{J_{p_{U}}E^{\star}q_{U}-J_{p_{V}}E^{\star}q_{V}\}-\{J_{p_{U}}U^{\star}J_{q_{U}}Ep_{U}-J_{p_{V}}V^{\star}J_{q_{V}}Ep_{V}\}, and applying the same ingredients used to prove the bound on ‖ ( A U − A V ) ∣ L 0 1 ‖ 1 → 1 \|(A_{U}-A_{V})\mid_{L_{0}^{1}}\|_{1\to 1} . Combining these estimates, we obtain ‖ D ​ p 𝖭𝖫 ​ ( U ) ​ [ E ] − D ​ p 𝖭𝖫 ​ ( V ) ​ [ E ] ‖ 1 \displaystyle\|Dp_{\mathsf{NL}}(U)[E]-Dp_{\mathsf{NL}}(V)[E]\|_{1} ≤ ‖ ( A U ∣ L 0 1 ) − 1 ‖ 1 → 1 ​ ( ‖ ( A U − A V ) ∣ L 0 1 ‖ 1 → 1 ​ ‖ ( A V ∣ L 0 1 ) − 1 ‖ 1 → 1 ​ ‖ h V , E ‖ 1 + ‖ h U , E − h V , E ‖ 1 ) \displaystyle\leq\|(A_{U}\mid_{L_{0}^{1}})^{-1}\|_{1\to 1}\Bigl(\|(A_{U}-A_{V})\mid_{L_{0}^{1}}\|_{1\to 1}\|(A_{V}\mid_{L_{0}^{1}})^{-1}\|_{1\to 1}\|h_{V,E}\|_{1}+\|h_{U,E}-h_{V,E}\|_{1}\Bigr) ≤ c ⁡ ( 1 + ‖ U ‖ ⊕ c + ‖ V ‖ ⊕ c ) ​ ‖ U − V ‖ ∞ ​ ‖ E ‖ ∞ . \displaystyle\leq c\bigl(1+\|U\|_{\oplus}^{c}+\|V\|_{\oplus}^{c}\bigr)\|U-V\|_{\infty}\|E\|_{\infty}. Taking the supremum over ‖ E ‖ ∞ ≤ 1 \|E\|_{\infty}\leq 1 completes the proof for D ​ p 𝖭𝖫 Dp_{\mathsf{NL}} . ∎ Corollary D.14 (Uniform Fréchet differentiability for NLHF) . For any fixed constant R ≥ 0 R\geq 0 , lim ‖ E ‖ ∞ → 0 sup ‖ U ‖ ⊕ ≤ R ‖ p 𝖭𝖫 ​ ( U + E ) − p 𝖭𝖫 ​ ( U ) − D ​ p 𝖭𝖫 ​ ( U ) ​ [ E ] ‖ 1 ‖ E ‖ ∞ = 0 \lim_{\|E\|_{\infty}\to 0}\sup_{\|U\|_{\oplus}\leq R}\frac{\|p_{\mathsf{NL}}(U+E)-p_{\mathsf{NL}}(U)-Dp_{\mathsf{NL}}(U)[E]\|_{1}}{\|E\|_{\infty}}=0 Proof. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2606.22652v1 [cs.LG] 21 Jun 2026 A Markov Chain Approach to Preference Alignment Takuya Koriyama Affiliation: The University of Chicago Tengyuan Liang Affiliation: The University of Chicago August 24, 2026 Abstract We propose Markov Chain from Human Feedback (MCHF), an elementary approach for aligning generative models from pairwise human preferences. Unlike Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), which reduces comparisons to a scalar reward, and Nash Learning from Human Feedback (NLHF), which preserves pairwise utilities through a KL-regularized minimax optimization, MCHF uses pairwise preferences directly to define a transition mechanism over model outputs. Given a pairwise utility U ⁡ ( x , y ) U(x,y) , which quantifies human preference for y y over x x , and a reference probability distribution μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}} , we define a Markov kernel 𝖯 ⁡ ( x , d ​ y ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( U ⁡ ( x , y ) ) ​ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ ( d ​ y ) \mathsf{P}(x,dy)\propto\exp(U(x,y))\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}(dy) , and take the Markov chain starting from μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}} as an iterative alignment procedure. We show that MCHF converges geometrically fast to the stationary distribution, with a convergence rate governed by the seminorm ‖ U ‖ ⊕ = inf g , f ∈ L ∞ ​ ( μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) ‖ U − g ⊕ f ‖ ∞ \|U\|_{\oplus}=\inf_{g,f\in L^{\infty}(\mu_{\mathsf{ref}})}\|U-g\oplus f\|_{\infty} , which quantifies the non-transitive structure of the pairwise utility. We further show that a mirror-descent algorithm for NLHF satisfies an analogous structure-adaptive convergence guarantee. Finally, through a perturbation analysis, we prove that when ‖ U ‖ ⊕ \|U\|_{\oplus} is small, MCHF and NLHF agree up to first order around an RLHF solution, which yields a unified view of reward-based, game-theoretic, and Markovian approaches to alignment. In particular, for two natural algorithms that converge to the MCHF/NLHF equilibria, we show that the first step of MCHF and NLHF recovers the RLHF solution based on the column-sum reward f ^ ​ ( y ) = ∫ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ ( 𝑑 x ) ​ U ​ ( x , y ) \hat{f}(y)=\int\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}(dx)U(x,y) , and starting from the second iteration, both algorithms incorporate the same linear functional of the residual U − ( − f ^ ) ⊕ f ^ U-(-\hat{f})\oplus\hat{f} , which captures the non-transitive structure of the pairwise utility U U . 1 Introduction Aligning AI systems with human preferences has become a central problem in modern machine learning, as large generative models are increasingly deployed in practical applications ( OpenAI, 2023 ; Gemini Team, Google, 2025 ; Anthropic, 2024 ) . In many alignment pipelines, human feedback is provided in the form of pairwise comparisons: given two candidate outputs, a human evaluator indicates which one is preferred. Such preference data are often easier to collect and prove more reliable than absolute numerical scores, as argued in several widely used alignment methods. 1.1 Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) In Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), pairwise comparisons are typically used to fit a scalar reward model, often through a probabilistic preference model such as the Bradley–Terry or Luce (BTL) model ( Bradley and Terry, 1952 ; Luce, 1959 ) : 𝒫 ⁡ ( x ≺ y ) = σ sigmoid ​ ( R ⁡ ( y ) − R ⁡ ( x ) ) where σ sigmoid ​ ( t ) ≡ ( 1 + e − t ) − 1 . \displaystyle\mathcal{P}(x\prec y)=\sigma_{	ext{sigmoid}}(R(y)-R(x))\quad	ext{where}\quad\sigma_{	ext{sigmoid}}(t)\equiv(1+e^{-t})^{-1}. (1) More precisely, given samples of pairwise comparisons { x i ≺ y i } i = 1 n \{x_{i}\prec y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} , assuming that they are drawn from the BTL model, one estimates the reward function R R by maximum likelihood estimation. The policy is then optimized against the learned reward R ^ \hat{R} , usually with a KL regularization term that keeps it close to a reference model μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}} ( Christiano et al., 2017 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Bai et al., 2022 ) : μ 𝖱𝖫 = argmax μ ( ∫ μ ⁡ ( 𝑑 x ) ​ R ^ ​ ( x ) − D 𝖪𝖫 ​ ( μ ∣ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) ) or μ 𝖱𝖫 ​ ( 𝑑 y ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( R ^ ​ ( y ) ) ​ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ ( 𝑑 y ) \displaystyle{\mu}_{\mathsf{RL}}=\argmax_{\mu}\Bigl(\int\mu(dx)\hat{R}(x)-D_{\mathsf{KL}}(\mu\mid\mu_{\mathsf{ref}})\Bigr)\quad	ext{or}\quad\mu_{\mathsf{RL}}(dy)\propto\exp(\hat{R}(y))\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}(dy) In practice, this problem is often solved approximately using reinforcement-learning algorithms such as proximal policy optimization (PPO) ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) . More recently, several variants and alternatives to the standard RLHF pipeline have been proposed; see Rafailov et al. (2023) ; Ethayarajh et al. (2024) ; Meng et al. (2024) ; Gheshlaghi Azar et al. (2024) ; Huang et al. (2025) , among others. Although a variety of RLHF-style methods have been proposed, their ultimate goal remains to aggregate pairwise preference information to a single scalar reward and then tilt the reference distribution by the reward. At its core, the reward modeling relies on the strong assumption that human preference is determined by the single reward, as in the BTL model assumption ( 1 ), which imposes a strong structural restriction on the preference structure 𝒫 ⁡ ( x ≺ y ) \mathcal{P}(x\prec y) . In particular, such a model cannot capture genuinely cyclic preference patterns such as 𝒫 ⁡ ( x ≺ y ) > 1 / 2 , 𝒫 ⁡ ( y ≺ z ) > 1 / 2 , 𝒫 ⁡ ( z ≺ x ) > 1 / 2 \mathcal{P}(x\prec y)>1/2,\mathcal{P}(y\prec z)>1/2,\mathcal{P}(z\prec x)>1/2 . Furthermore, RLHF-style methods assume the existence of a single reward function representing aggregated human preference. In practice, preferences may vary across human annotators, and therefore cannot always be faithfully summarized by a homogeneous reward model. This limitation has motivated pluralistic alignment in the community, which tries to account for heterogeneous preferences explicitly ( Sorensen et al., 2024 ) . 1.2 Nash Learning from Human Feedback (NLHF): a Game-Theoretic Approach There have been a variety of attempts at incorporating preference information directly, without introducing an explicit single reward model. Among them, one influential example is the Nash Learning from Human Feedback (NLHF) ( Munos et al., 2024 ) . The key idea is to first learn the preference model ( x , y ) ↦ 𝒫 ⁡ ( x ≺ y ) (x,y)\mapsto\mathcal{P}(x\prec y) directly from a dataset of comparisons { x i ≺ y i } i = 1 n \{x_{i}\prec y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} , for instance by solving max ⁡ ∑ i = 1 n θ ⁡ log ⁡ 𝒫 θ ​ ( x i ≺ y i ) \max_{	heta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{P}_{	heta}(x_{i}\prec y_{i}) where { 𝒫 θ : 𝒳 × 𝒳 → [ 0 , 1 ] } \{\mathcal{P}_{	heta}:\mathcal{X}	imes\mathcal{X}	o[0,1]\} is a parametric class, typically represented by 𝒫 θ ​ ( x ≺ y ) = sigmoid ​ ( U θ ​ ( x , y ) ) \mathcal{P}_{	heta}(x\prec y)=	ext{sigmoid}(U_{	heta}(x,y)) (or more generally 𝒫 θ = Φ ∘ U θ \mathcal{P}_{	heta}=\Phi\circ U_{	heta} for an increasing link function Φ \Phi mapping to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] ), where U θ U_{	heta} is a neural network. Notice that when we further parametrize U θ U_{	heta} in additive form, U θ ​ ( x , y ) = − R θ ​ ( x ) + R θ ​ ( y ) U_{	heta}(x,y)=-R_{	heta}(x)+R_{	heta}(y) , then it is equivalent to the reward modelling by BTL model used in the RLHF pipeline. Given such a pairwise utility function U = U θ U=U_{	heta} , NLHF defines the aligned distribution through the following minimax optimization problem μ 𝖭𝖫 ∈ argmax μ min ν ​ ∬ ν ⁡ ( 𝑑 x ) ​ μ ​ ( 𝑑 y ) ​ U ​ ( x , y ) − D 𝖪𝖫 ​ ( μ ∣ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) + D 𝖪𝖫 ​ ( ν ∣ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ) . \displaystyle{\mu}_{\mathsf{NL}}\in\argmax_{\mu}\min_{

More broadly, game-theoretic perspectives on alignment have led to formulations based on other solution concepts, such as Stackelberg games ( Pásztor et al., 2026 ; Chu et al., 2026 ) and multiplayer games ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . The NLHF paper ( Munos et al., 2024 ) argues that the Nash-equilibrium formulation is attractive because it can yield a more diverse distribution than reward-based alignment methods. A more refined analysis of this phenomenon has been developed through the lens of social choice theory (cf. Gölz et al. (2026) ; Shi et al. (2025) ). Nevertheless, because NLHF is formulated as a worst-case equilibrium against an adversarial opponent, it is intrinsically more pessimistic than reward-based alignment, and it is not always clear that such a pessimistic objective is the most appropriate one for fine-tuning generative models. Moreover, NLHF treats alignment as a simultaneous game, in which the two players, μ \mu and ν 
u , optimize a regularized zero-sum objective at the same time. In contrast, preference refinement can be more naturally viewed as a non-simultaneous, leader-follower procedure: given a current output, one samples a new output conditionally on it, favoring alternatives that are preferred to the current one. Figure 1: Workflow of alignment. We start from pairwise preference data, then we either construct a reward function (usually based on the BTL model) and run RLHF or construct a directed weighted graph and run MCHF (our proposal) or NLHF. Here, unlike the scalar reward, the weighted graph can preserve non-transitive/pairwise interaction structure in human preferences, and therefore MCHF/NLHF provide more flexible alignment methods than RLHF. 1.3 Our contribution: a Markov Chain Approach Motivated by this viewpoint, we propose Markov Chain from Human Feedback (MCHF), a Markovian alignment approach that uses pairwise preference utilities directly through such a non-simultaneous formulation. Concretely, given a utility U ⁡ ( x , y ) U(x,y) , where larger values indicate that y y is preferred to x x , and a reference model μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}} , we define the Markov kernel 𝖯 \mathsf{P} by 𝖯 ⁡ ( x , d ​ y ) = exp ⁡ ( U ⁡ ( x , y ) ) Z ⁡ ( x ) ​ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ ( d ​ y ) , \mathsf{P}(x,dy)= rac{\exp(U(x,y))}{Z(x)}\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}(dy), where Z ⁡ ( x ) Z(x) is the normalizing constant. Then, given a current distribution μ \mu , one step of MCHF updates it according to μ new ​ ( 𝑑 y ) = μ ​ 𝖯 ​ ( 𝑑 y ) = ∫ μ ⁡ ( 𝑑 x ) ​ 𝖯 ​ ( x , 𝑑 y ) . \mu_{	ext{new}}(dy)=\mu\mathsf{P}(dy)=\int\mu(dx)\mathsf{P}(x,dy). Here, the kernel 𝖯 \mathsf{P} favors transitions from a current output x x to outputs y y that are preferred relative to x x , while the reference distribution μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}} preserves the structure, especially the support, of the reference distribution μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}} . Thus, in contrast to the simultaneous-game interpretation underlying NLHF, MCHF implements a non-simultaneous/leader-follower alignment procedure via the conditional sampling from the Markov kernel 𝖯 \mathsf{P} . This one-step update can also be iterated, starting from μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}} : μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ↦ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ 𝖯 ↦ μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ 𝖯 2 ↦ ⋯ → μ 𝗋𝖾𝖿 ​ 𝖯 ∞ = μ 𝖬𝖢 \mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\mapsto\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\mathsf{P}\mapsto\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\mathsf{P}^{2}\mapsto\cdots	o\mu_{\mathsf{ref}}\mathsf{P}^{\infty}=\mu_{\mathsf{MC}} Then, MCHF induces an interpolation path from the reference distribution to the stationary distribution μ 𝖬𝖢 \mu_{\mathsf{MC}} , which fully incorporates the pairwise preference utility U U . This iterative alignment procedure is inspired by classical spectral rank-aggregation methods ( Brin and Page, 1998 ; Negahban et al., 2017 ) , where one constructs a directed graph from pairwise comparisons and represents an aggregate ranking as the stationary distribution of a Markov chain on the graph (see Figure 1 ).
